content.text: By morning, Astalor had built a mouth into the cage.

The device hung between two of the surviving pylons: a narrow ring of crimson metal inscribed with channels too fine to see until power entered them. Three conduits ran from the ring to a waist-high receiving frame. Beyond it, M’uru turned within the restraint field, white-gold radiance sliding through the bands in slow pulses.

The Sunfury command ward had been cleared of everyone without a stated purpose. Kael’thas stood at the forward line with Rommath and Liadrin. Lord Sanguinar watched from his right, one hand resting on his sword. Daric, Althene, Selorien, and the officers of the Silvermoon retinue waited behind them with the bruised stillness of soldiers who had slept in armor.

Falanaras felt every magical current in the ward. The cage pressed outward with immense contained force. The receiving frame waited empty. Beneath both ran the ordinary pulse of the camp’s fel-fed defenses, familiar enough to ignore. M’uru’s presence made that green power feel coarse against his senses.

“Containment loss remained beneath one part in twelve thousand through the night,” Astalor said. He had acquired a fresh burn along his left wrist and seemed pleased by it. “Ambient output recovered after every measurement. The source displays no measurable fatigue from restraint alone.”
“Restraint was never the claim we came to prove,” Kael’thas said.

He looked rested despite the cut on his cheek. His crimson mantle had been replaced, his high shoulder guard polished free of battle soot. The three Verdant Spheres moved behind him with their habitual fire restored. Victory had already been made presentable.

Astalor touched the receiving frame. Red lines woke along its rim. “The first draw will remain narrow. Captain Falanaras can interrupt the channel if the current exceeds tolerance. Lady Liadrin will assess its nature. I will govern duration.”
Liadrin’s gaze stayed on M’uru. “Who receives it?”
Kael’thas extended one hand toward Falanaras. “The captain asked the correct questions before the assault. Let him help answer them.”

Falanaras stepped through the line. He had drained hostile spells in battle since his first months of formal training. He knew the intake of arcane force, the oily heat of fel, the cold pressure of necromancy. Each demanded a different posture, yet all could be caught, measured, and made useful.
Nothing in that knowledge told him how to take hold of the Light.
He placed his palm inside the ring. The metal was warm. Liadrin moved beside him, close enough that the edge of her gauntlet touched his wrist.
“Do not reach as you would for an enemy spell,” she said. “Let the channel bring it to you.”
“You make that sound simple.”
“It was, once.”
Astalor opened the channel.

M’uru’s radiance tightened toward the nearest pylon. White fire entered the crimson conduit and ran through the frame. The first touch struck Falanaras behind the breastbone. His lungs opened on a breath he had not known he was holding. Warmth passed into his blood, through the old ache in his bones, and into the hollow place the Sunwell had left.
The hunger vanished.

For three heartbeats he remembered what it was to live without constant ache. No ration waited at the edge of thought. No active ward drew a portion of his attention. Power gathered in him with a clarity that asked for movement: a shield raised over wounded soldiers, a blade bright against the undead, strength carried where ordinary flesh would fail.
Then M’uru cried out.

The sound held no voice, but pain needed none. A chord broke across the ward and drove several soldiers back a step. M’uru’s revolving limbs shuddered. The white center of its body dimmed around the channel, then surged as the captive tried to restore what had been taken.
Falanaras jerked his hand away. The channel clung to him in a bright thread until Astalor cut it.
Silence followed. It lasted only long enough for everyone present to understand what the device had done.
Astalor studied the gauges. “Yield exceeded the upper estimate by thirty-one percent. Recovery has begun.”
“Captain?” Rommath asked.
Falanaras closed his hand. Light remained beneath his skin, responsive and immense. “The ache is gone. I can hold the power. It wants expression more than storage.”
Liadrin watched him with an intensity that made the ward fall away. “Call it.”

He thought of Edric in the Ghostlands, breath measured behind a lifted shield. Falanaras raised his empty hand. The stolen Light answered in a red-gold flare that spread over his forearm and hardened into a narrow barrier. It lasted a single breath before breaking into sparks.
The officers stirred. Sanguinar smiled.
M’uru brightened again within the cage. Astalor compared the restored radiance to his first reading, then turned the gauge so Kael’thas could see.
“No measurable depletion,” he said. “The pain response is immediate. The loss is not.”
Kael’thas faced the gathered blood elves. “Again. Lower duration. We will learn what we have won.”

They came in turn. A wounded Sunfury lieutenant received enough to stand without favoring her bandaged leg. Daric drew a narrow current and produced a burst of radiance across his damaged shield, then stared at the metal as if it had betrayed an expectation. Althene accepted the test without ceremony and sent a bright thread along the length of an arrow before dismissing it.
Each draw hurt M’uru. Each ended with the captive’s light returning to its prior strength.

When Liadrin placed her hand inside the ring, the naaru’s tones changed before Astalor opened the conduit. She went rigid. White radiance crossed the space between them, entered the apparatus, and poured into her with enough force to drive one knee against the ground.
Falanaras reached for her shoulder. She caught his wrist and held him away.

The Light gathered around Liadrin as it had around no one else. It traced the edges of her black armor, filled the old sunburst engraved beneath later scoring, and burned from her eyes. Her face twisted with pain or fury; Falanaras could not separate them.
“Enough,” Astalor said, and closed the channel.
Liadrin remained kneeling until the last radiance withdrew beneath her skin. Then she rose under her own strength.
Kael’thas regarded her with open calculation. “You held more than the others.”
“I knew it once,” Liadrin said. “My body remembers what faith no longer grants.”
The discussion moved into the command pavilion while guards closed around M’uru.

Astalor covered the central table with readings. His notes reduced pain, radiance, recovery, and mortal tolerance to columns that could be compared. Selorien stood behind him and quietly replaced the bloodstained cloth around his wrist before it dripped onto the figures.

“Direct access through a common reservoir would fail,” Astalor said. “Too many simultaneous draws would create surges, contamination, and loss. That does not make broad relief impossible. It means the city will need buffers, separate channels, and a way to regulate demand. These individual trials give me the tolerances from which to build them.”

Rommath leaned over the record of M’uru’s recovery. “An individual transfer proves the source can relieve the hunger. The kingdom needs a method that does not depend on selecting one recipient at a time.”

“Agreed. The individual recipient is an instrument of study, not the final scale.” Astalor tapped Liadrin’s result. “This is the strongest transfer by a wide margin. Her prior bond provides a channel the rest of us lack. If we understand why, we may learn how to move the power safely into less responsive vessels—and eventually into the city’s wards.”

Liadrin stood at the table’s end. The Light had left her pale, though her voice remained steady. “Priests once carried the Light to the wounded. Paladins carried it into battle. We have soldiers enough, and no shortage of wounds.”
Sanguinar gave a low laugh. “Then make paladins.”
Liadrin looked at him. “Paladins are formed through devotion. Whatever we make from this will answer to discipline.”
“Better,” Sanguinar said.

Falanaras remembered Edric’s revulsion in the Ghostlands and the barrier that had answered his own hand moments ago. The power itself had felt pure. Its path into him had been an injury done to someone else.

“A military cadre could test healing, warding, and force under controlled conditions while the distribution work continues,” Rommath said. “It would give us disciplined recipients, reliable records, and defenders who no longer draw on the failing stores needed by the rest of the kingdom.”

Kael’thas walked to the pavilion opening. M’uru’s cage shone beyond the canvas, surrounded by soldiers and siege wreckage. “Quel’Thalas once waited for sacred power to judge us worthy. That patience brought only blood. We did not take this prize to ease the hunger of a favored few.”

He turned back. “Take M’uru home. Learn how its power can reach our infirmaries, ration halls, public wards, and every household the old Sunwell once sustained. Until that method exists, use controlled recipients to prove what the Light can do. If the same work gives our people warriors who can wield it without heaven’s approval, we will use that strength as well.”

No name followed the command. No oath, uniform, or doctrine existed yet. Still, attention shifted toward Liadrin. She had borne more of the stolen Light than anyone present, and she alone understood what its old service had required.
She accepted their scrutiny without lowering her eyes. “If soldiers are chosen, they must know what stands beneath their power. Forgetting will make appetite of duty.”
“Teach them, then,” Kael’thas said.
Liadrin’s mouth tightened. “First Astalor must learn how to give them the power without killing them.”
Astalor gathered his readings. “Two problems, then: distribution without collapse and recipients without death. At least they share an apparatus.”
They left Netherstorm under a victory order that forbade celebration.

Sunfury translocators carried the retinue and M’uru’s frame from the staging grounds to a secured platform in Hellfire Peninsula. The transfer took six linked casts and most of a day. At every arrival, Astalor counted pylons before people. Selorien counted both and supplied whichever total Astalor had neglected.

M’uru passed over Outland wrapped in false darkness. Layered veils concealed the white radiance, though they could not silence its tones. Soldiers assigned to the transport learned to speak only when necessary. The sound entered conversation and made ordinary words feel disrespectful.

At the final Hellfire station, Falanaras looked back toward the road they had crossed weeks earlier. The red waste ran beneath a sky split by distant fire. Somewhere beyond it lay Zangarmarsh, Blade’s Edge, the Netherstorm camp, and the fortress they had broken open. The distances had seemed large while they marched. Now secrecy folded them into a chain of guarded rooms.
Daric joined him beside the Portal approach. A new shield rode on his back, Sunfury issue and too ornate for his taste.
“I preferred the ship,” he said.
“You complained about the ship.”
“I had not yet acquired perspective.” Daric glanced toward the shrouded cage. “Will you tell them at home?”
“What part?”
“That it came willingly. That it screamed when we tested it. That it works.”
Falanaras watched magisters widen the Portal’s stabilizing field around the transport frame. “If I tell the truth, I tell all three.”
Daric considered that. “You did acquire something in Outland.”
“A captaincy.”
“I was going to say an alarming tolerance for impossible answers.”

The shrouded frame entered the Dark Portal between two files of spellbreakers. Falanaras crossed beside the left forward pylon. Netherstorm’s pressure vanished behind him. The Blasted Lands received them with barren wind and a night sky whose stars held their proper places.

Home lay far to the north, but Rommath had prepared the last road before they departed. Inside the blood-elf-held fortifications, a relay chamber waited beneath wards keyed to his authority. Its receiving circle opened onto a sealed magisterial vault below Silvermoon.

The spell took every magister in the retinue and twelve stationed at the Portal. Crimson light rose around M’uru’s prison. For one instant Falanaras saw the naaru through all its veils, brilliant enough to throw shadows across two worlds.
Then dry wind became cool stone, and the air smelled of silverleaf incense, lamp oil, and home.

The receiving vault had been emptied except for guards. Theron Brightshield stood in the first rank with a restored shield on his arm. Lethira waited above him on a narrow gallery, bow drawn toward the arriving frame until she recognized the figures within the light.
Theron’s scarred face changed by less than a smile. It was enough.
Lethira lowered her bow. “You were meant to bring back a report.”
“The report required containment pylons.”
“Naturally.” She looked at M’uru’s veiled radiance. The sarcasm left her face. “What did you bring us?”

Before Falanaras could answer, the far doors opened and Lor’themar Theron entered with Halduron Brightwing and a guard of senior magisters. The Regent Lord wore no ceremonial mantle. He had come dressed for an interrupted night, his hair bound back, his expression already fixed on the work ahead.
Rommath bowed. “Regent Lord. By order of Prince Kael’thas, we deliver the answer secured from Tempest Keep.”
Lor’themar looked through the veils. M’uru’s tones moved through the vault, soft enough to raise the hairs along Falanaras’s arms.
“An answer to which question?” Lor’themar asked.
The council convened before the transport wards had cooled.

They met in an adjoining chamber built for supply disputes and emergency command. Its table still bore old knife marks from the defense of the city. Lor’themar took the head. Halduron stood at his right, Rommath at his left. Astalor arranged his instruments without waiting to be invited. Liadrin remained near the closed door to M’uru’s vault.
Falanaras had expected to be dismissed with the other field officers. Lor’themar kept him, Theron, and Lethira as witnesses to the arrival and representatives of the soldiers now guarding it.
“Begin with custody,” Lor’themar said. “Who owns the prisoner?”
Rommath’s reply came without pause. “Prince Kael’thas seized M’uru through force of arms and sent it for the preservation of Quel’Thalas.”
“That tells me who gave the order. Here, beneath a city I am charged to govern, who controls access?”
“The magisters maintain containment,” Astalor said. “Military guards secure the approaches. Lady Liadrin will advise on Light exposure.”
“Under whose authority?”
Astalor looked to Rommath. Rommath looked to Lor’themar.
“Mine,” the Regent Lord said. “The prince’s purpose will be honored. Silvermoon will not contain an unknown power beneath its streets through divided command.”
Rommath inclined his head. “Agreed.”
Halduron folded his arms. “If the cage fails?”
“M’uru could have broken it during capture,” Falanaras said. “It chose not to.”
Every face turned toward him. Theron’s did not move, but Falanaras felt his attention sharpen.
Lor’themar rested both hands on the table. “You brought into my city a prisoner powerful enough to escape and unwilling to do so.”
“Yes,” Liadrin said.
“Do you know why?”
“No.”
The honesty settled heavily. Lor’themar shifted to Astalor. “What happens when you draw from it?”

“The recipient gains usable Holy power and immediate relief from magical withdrawal. M’uru experiences pain. Its output returns to baseline within moments. Ambient diffusion is already easing symptoms near the vault, but we do not yet know how to regulate or extend it.”
Lethira’s fingers tightened around the strap of her bow. “You tested that more than once.”
“Repetition established recovery,” Astalor said.
“Pain also appears repeatable.”
Astalor met her stare. “Yes.”
Lor’themar did not rebuke either of them. “Who knows?”
Rommath listed the Outland command, the transport teams, the Portal garrison, and the Silvermoon guards. The number was already too large for permanent silence.

“Then we control the truth before rumor supplies a worse one,” Lor’themar said. “The city will be told that the prince has sent a new magical resource under study. No location. No access. No promise of a ration before you can deliver one. The work remains directed toward public relief, and the reports will state whether it is approaching that goal.”
“And the nature of the resource?” Halduron asked.

Lor’themar looked toward the sealed vault. “Anyone who draws from a living prisoner should know the source. Anyone merely passing through the market does not need a riot handed to them before breakfast.”

Rommath’s expression remained hard. “The primary application is relief throughout the kingdom. That requires a distribution method we do not yet possess. A trained military cadre can be developed in parallel: controlled recipients for the research and defenders who can wield the Light without devotional dependence.”
Halduron looked at Liadrin. “Under you?”
“If the method can be made survivable,” she said. “If those chosen can obey a limit. If they understand that effectiveness does not alter the source of what they carry.”
Theron spoke for the first time. “Does it work against the undead?”
“It is the Light,” Liadrin said. “Yes.”
Theron nodded once. Falanaras knew that motion. His friend had placed the horror and the utility beside each other and begun considering where a shield might stand between them.

Lor’themar saw it too. Weariness crossed his face before discipline removed it. “You will submit a containment plan by noon, a distribution program and trial protocol by tomorrow. No further draws tonight. The guards rotate every two hours. Anyone who enters that vault is named in writing.”
Astalor began to object to the delay. Rommath silenced him with a glance.

“The prince sent us salvation,” Lor’themar said. “It arrived as a military prisoner, a religious crisis, and an apparatus that can injure half the city if mishandled. Permit me one night to govern it.”
By afternoon, Silvermoon had begun to absorb the secret.

Magisters closed three lower passages for “structural repair.” Supply carts moved under guard through service streets. A notice praised Kael’thas’s victory in Outland and promised that a new source of power had reached the kingdom for study. Citizens gathered beneath the posted words and argued over how soon study should become ration.

The city had practice receiving necessities with dangerous names. Fel crystals already burned green above restored avenues. Mana distribution queues formed beside buildings whose carvings still honored the Sunwell. Children learned which public wards eased the ache and which alleys held people who had stopped choosing limits.

M’uru entered that life unseen. Its presence traveled through stone as a low warmth. Guards stationed nearest the vault reported easier breathing and steadier hands. One kitchen worker sat down on a stair and wept because the hunger had receded for the first time in years, though she did not know why.

The effect weakened with distance. Two levels above the vault, a guard could still feel it as warmth behind the eyes. At street level it became no more than an easier breath, readily mistaken for a strong ward or a generous ration. Even that was enough to alter behavior. Soldiers due to rotate away found reasons to finish reports slowly. A pair of laborers volunteered twice to carry conduit housings into the lower halls. Their foreman sent them back to the loading yard before gratitude became loitering.

The first rumor named the source as a cleansed fel crystal large enough to power a district. The second claimed Rommath had recovered a fragment of the Sunwell. By midday, a jeweler near the Royal Exchange was selling brass pendants stamped with a sunburst and promising that they would attune themselves when the prince’s gift entered public service.

Lor’themar’s clerks confiscated the pendants for fraudulent enchantment and left the rumor untouched. Denial would have given it an official spine. Silence allowed a dozen competing hopes to exhaust one another.

Below, the guards learned the harder facts. They heard M’uru’s tones through the sealed doors and felt the containment bands answer in their teeth. Those who had served before the fall stood straighter when the radiance passed beneath the threshold. One former temple sentry requested reassignment without naming a reason. Another placed both hands against the door after his watch ended and remained there until Theron told him quietly that reverence did not grant entry.

Theron reported each incident in the plain language Lor’themar had ordered: time, name, action, disposition. Lethira took the upper approaches with rangers who trusted stone corridors less than open sight lines. She found two magisterial apprentices tracing the outer wards from a ventilation court and sent them away with such inventive predictions of disciplinary labor that neither returned.

None of it resembled the celebration at the Sunfury camp. The city met M’uru through rosters, sealed passages, diverted deliveries, and the faint relief of people who did not know why their hands had steadied. The captive’s suffering remained below ground. Its usefulness rose invisibly through the floors.

That division unsettled Falanaras more than open approval would have. In Outland, everyone who accepted the Light had heard M’uru cry. Silvermoon might receive the benefit at a distance, softened by official language and several layers of stone. Lor’themar had insisted that future wielders know the source, but knowledge could still become ritual phrasing—repeated correctly, felt less each time.

Astalor’s work already extended beyond prospective soldiers. In adjoining chambers, magisters fed traces of M’uru’s ambient radiance into wardstones, healing foci, and empty mana vessels. One stone held a weak warmth for eleven minutes. Two crystals clouded from within. A conduit meant to carry the current toward the nearest infirmary bled half its charge into the surrounding walls before Selorien shut it down.

Rommath’s clerks spread maps beside the instruments. Their inked routes ran outward from the vault toward clinics, ration stations, barracks, workshops, and the common quarters where weak crystals served too many households. Every route remained hypothetical, branching across the city in red ink.

Liadrin did not leave the lower complex. When Falanaras passed the vault on his way to final debriefing, he saw her through the open inspection door, standing beyond the apparatus with her helmet beneath one arm. Astalor’s magisters moved around her, measuring and marking. She watched M’uru without prayer and without retreat. The posture carried the same severity she had shown in the shrine: responsibility maintained through attention.

When Falanaras emerged from final debriefing into evening, Silvermoon’s towers caught the last sun in gold and crimson. Repaired bridges arched over streets where merchants closed their awnings and ward-lamps woke one by one. After Outland, the city seemed impossibly delicate. After Tempest Keep, it seemed defenseless against what had been placed beneath it.

Theron and Lethira waited outside the barracks court. Someone had found Falanaras a fresh uniform, but Netherstorm dust remained in the seams of his boots. Lethira noticed before offering him her forearm.
“You look offensive,” she said.
“Outland has lower standards.”
“That is the first credible report you have given me.”
Theron clasped his shoulder. The grip was careful around an injury Falanaras had stopped noticing. “Welcome home.”

The words reached somewhere the cheering had not. Falanaras looked past them toward the barracks windows, the familiar training court, the wall where Rynel had once corrected his stance with a wooden staff and an insult. Home had continued without him. He had returned carrying an answer large enough to alter it.

They found a quiet place on the western terrace, where reconstruction ended against the ruins. Beyond the rail, broken foundations descended toward the dark scar of the lost quarter. Lethira produced three cups and a bottle that tasted of berries, smoke, and someone’s impatience with proper aging.
“Tell us what the notice does not,” Theron said.

Falanaras told them about the road across Outland, the naga in Zangarmarsh, the fel creatures in Blade’s Edge, and the blood elves at Kael’thas’s camp who had learned to count demons among useful allies. He described the assault in fragments because a whole account would have sounded less true. Daric’s shield. Althene’s bridge. Selorien dragging a wounded hauler away from a failing pylon.
Then he told them about M’uru.
Lethira listened without interruption until he described the first draw. “It hurt.”
“Yes.”
“And you did it again.”
“We needed to know whether the first result was stable.” The answer came too quickly. It carried Astalor’s cadence, stripped of his elegance.
Lethira looked toward the city. “There you are.”
“Where?”
“Somewhere past the point where you used to admit a thing was terrible before explaining why you did it.” Her tone stayed dry, yet concern had entered beneath it. “Outland taught you efficiency.”
Falanaras wanted to deny it. Instead he remembered the receiving ring, the instant of perfect relief, and how readily he had raised a barrier from another being’s pain.
Theron turned his cup between both hands. “Does it work?”
“Yes.”
“Well?”
Falanaras opened his hand. A faint red-gold gleam remained in the creases of his palm, though hours had passed since the test. “Well enough to change how we fight. Perhaps how we live.”
Theron studied the light. His face held no wonder. Only the practical attention he gave a damaged shield that might still save someone if repaired correctly.
“Rynel could have used that,” he said.
The thought had followed Falanaras across two worlds. “Yes.”
“Would it have saved him?” Lethira asked.
“I do not know.” Falanaras closed his hand over the glow. “I know it could save the next one.”

Below the terrace, ward-lamps brightened along the avenue. Citizens moved through their evening routines with mana crystals in pockets and green light above their heads. Few knew what slept beneath the city. None knew what name its power would eventually take.
Lethira poured the last of the bottle. “You are home,” she said. “Try to remain recognizable.”

Falanaras looked from her to Theron. Familiar faces, familiar ruins, familiar hunger. Outland had changed the distance he could travel inside necessity before alarm caught up with him. His friends had seen it within an hour.
Under their feet, too deep for sound, M’uru’s presence warmed the stone.
Silvermoon had taken another dangerous thing into itself and called the act survival. This time Falanaras had helped carry it home.
